sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited by a threat actor.

Security+ expects you to recognize vulnerabilities across applications, operating systems, web applications, hardware, virtualization, cloud environments, supply chains, cryptography, and mobile devices.
Use this sequence: identify where the weakness exists, determine what type of vulnerability it is, and find the clue that gives it away.
sections.callout: Vulnerability = the weakness · Exploit = the method used to take advantage of it

sections.title: Application Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Applications can contain weaknesses in their code, memory handling, timing, or update process. Security+ specifically calls out memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions, and malicious updates.
sections.callout: Ask which part of the application's behavior contains the weakness.

sections.title: Memory Injection and Buffer Overflow
paragraphs: Both vulnerabilities involve memory, but the defining problem is different.

entries.title: Memory Injection
paragraphs: Memory injection occurs when malicious code or instructions are inserted into the memory space of a running process. The attacker may try to make a legitimate process execute malicious activity.
entries.memoryHook: Put malicious code inside a running process.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious code inserted into process memory → Memory injection

entries.title: Buffer Overflow
paragraphs: A buffer temporarily holds data. A buffer overflow occurs when an application writes more data into a buffer than it was designed to hold. Excess data can overwrite nearby memory and cause crashes, corruption, unexpected behavior, or malicious code execution.
entries.memoryHook: Too much data for the container.
entries.recognitionCue: Input exceeds allocated memory space → Buffer overflow

table.caption: Memory vulnerability comparison
rows: Malicious code is placed into process memory
Too much data crosses a memory boundary

sections.title: Race Conditions and TOC/TOU
paragraphs: A race condition occurs when the result of an operation depends on the timing or order of multiple actions. An attacker tries to take advantage of a small timing window.

entries.title: Race Condition
paragraphs: Security depends on which of two competing actions happens first.
entries.memoryHook: The attacker wins the race between two operations.
entries.recognitionCue: Security depends on timing or operation order → Race condition

entries.title: Time-of-Check (TOC)
paragraphs: Time-of-check is the moment the system verifies that an object, condition, or permission is valid.
examples: The system checks whether a user has permission to access a file.
entries.recognitionCue: System validates the condition → TOC

entries.title: Time-of-Use (TOU)
paragraphs: Time-of-use is the later moment when the system uses the object or performs the operation.
examples: After checking permission, the system opens the file.
entries.recognitionCue: System performs the action after the check → TOU

entries.title: TOC/TOU Vulnerability
paragraphs: The vulnerability appears when something changes after the system checks it but before the system uses it.
entries.memoryHook: Check says safe → something changes → system uses the changed object.
entries.recognitionCue: Object changes between validation and use → TOC/TOU race condition

sections.title: Malicious Updates
paragraphs: A malicious update occurs when software that appears to be a trusted update contains malicious code. An attacker may compromise the software vendor, build process, update infrastructure, or update package itself.

entries.title: Malicious Update
paragraphs: The trusted delivery mechanism becomes the way malicious code reaches the customer.
entries.memoryHook: The trusted update became the attack.
entries.recognitionCue: Malware delivered through a trusted update process → Malicious update

sections.title: Operating System-Based Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: An operating system controls processes, files, memory, users, permissions, hardware access, and network services. A weakness in the OS can therefore affect a large portion of the system.
OS-based vulnerabilities can result from unpatched flaws, weak security settings, vulnerable services, or unsupported versions.

entries.title: Operating System-Based
paragraphs: The weakness exists in Windows, Linux, macOS, or another operating-system component rather than only in an individual application.
entries.recognitionCue: Security flaw in an operating-system component → OS-based vulnerability

sections.title: Web-Based Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Web applications constantly accept user input. If that input is handled insecurely, an attacker may make the application perform actions the developer never intended.
Security+ specifically includes SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

sections.title: SQL Injection and Cross-Site Scripting
paragraphs: SQL injection and XSS both begin with unsafe input handling, but they affect different destinations.

entries.title: Structured Query Language Injection (SQLi)
paragraphs: SQL injection occurs when malicious SQL commands are supplied as input and the application improperly passes them to a database. An attacker may read or change records, delete data, or bypass authentication.
entries.memoryHook: User input becomes a database command.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious input manipulates database queries → SQL injection

entries.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
paragraphs: Cross-site scripting occurs when malicious script content is delivered through a trusted web application and executes in another user's browser. It may steal session information, manipulate content, redirect users, or act through the victim's session.
entries.memoryHook: The website causes malicious script to run in the victim's browser.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious script executes in another user's browser → XSS

sections.title: Hardware Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Security weaknesses can exist in physical devices and the software embedded inside them. Security+ includes firmware, end-of-life status, and legacy technology.

entries.title: Firmware
paragraphs: Firmware is software embedded in hardware such as routers, motherboards, storage devices, and IoT equipment. Firmware can contain security flaws just like ordinary software.
entries.recognitionCue: Weakness in embedded device software → Firmware vulnerability

sections.title: End-of-Life and Legacy
paragraphs: These terms can overlap, but they describe different problems.

entries.title: End-of-Life
paragraphs: End-of-life means a product has reached the point where the manufacturer no longer provides normal support, patches, firmware updates, or vulnerability fixes. The product may still function even though new weaknesses can remain permanently unpatched.
entries.memoryHook: Still functioning does not mean still supported.
entries.recognitionCue: Vendor support and security fixes have ended → End-of-life

entries.title: Legacy
paragraphs: A legacy system is older technology an organization still depends on. It may require old applications, use outdated protocols, lack modern security features, or be difficult to replace.
entries.memoryHook: Old, but the business still needs it.
entries.recognitionCue: Older technology still required for operations → Legacy

sections.callout: End-of-life = vendor support ended · Legacy = older technology remains in use

sections.title: Virtualization Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Virtualization lets multiple virtual machines share physical infrastructure. That flexibility creates security concerns involving isolation and shared resources.

entries.title: Virtual Machine (VM) Escape
paragraphs: A VM escape occurs when an attacker breaks out of a guest virtual machine and reaches the hypervisor, host system, or other virtual machines.
entries.recognitionCue: Compromised guest reaches host or hypervisor → VM escape

entries.title: Resource Reuse
paragraphs: Virtual environments repeatedly assign memory, storage, and compute resources. If a resource is not properly cleared before reassignment, remnants of the previous user's data may remain.
entries.memoryHook: The new user receives traces of the previous user's data.
entries.recognitionCue: Residual information remains in a reassigned resource → Resource reuse

sections.title: Cloud-Specific Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Cloud environments introduce vulnerabilities related to how resources are shared, configured, accessed, and managed. Weaknesses may involve cloud permissions, APIs, storage configuration, identity controls, or multi-tenant environments.

entries.title: Cloud-Specific
paragraphs: The weakness arises from the architecture, configuration, or services of the cloud environment.
entries.recognitionCue: Weakness tied specifically to cloud architecture or services → Cloud-specific vulnerability

sections.title: Supply-Chain Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: An organization can inherit vulnerabilities through a company or product it already trusts. Security+ divides these into service-provider, hardware-provider, and software-provider vulnerabilities.

entries.title: Service Provider
paragraphs: A service provider may have privileged access or connectivity to customer systems. If that provider is compromised, its customers may also be exposed.
entries.recognitionCue: Trusted external service becomes the weakness → Service-provider vulnerability

entries.title: Hardware Provider
paragraphs: A hardware provider may introduce risk through compromised components, firmware, manufacturing, or distribution.
entries.memoryHook: The problem was introduced through the physical product.
entries.recognitionCue: Compromised hardware or component source → Hardware-provider vulnerability

entries.title: Software Provider
paragraphs: A software provider may be compromised through development systems, software packages, updates, or distribution infrastructure. Customers may then receive malicious or vulnerable software from a trusted source.
entries.recognitionCue: Trusted software or update source becomes compromised → Software-provider vulnerability

table.caption: Supply-chain vulnerability recognition sheet
rows: Compromise enters through a trusted external service
Compromise enters through a physical component or device
Compromise enters through trusted software or an update

sections.title: Cryptographic Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Cryptography can fail when weak algorithms are used, keys are too weak or poorly protected, implementations are flawed, or outdated methods remain in use.

entries.title: Cryptographic Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Using cryptography does not automatically mean the algorithm, key, or implementation is strong.
entries.recognitionCue: Weakness in an algorithm, key, or cryptographic implementation → Cryptographic vulnerability

sections.title: Misconfiguration
paragraphs: A misconfiguration occurs when a system or application is configured insecurely. Examples include excessive permissions, open services, publicly accessible storage, weak firewall rules, and unsafe settings.
The technology may work exactly as designed; the weakness exists because it was set up incorrectly.

entries.title: Misconfiguration
paragraphs: The security problem comes from incorrect settings rather than a broken feature.
entries.memoryHook: Nothing is broken. It was simply set up wrong.
entries.recognitionCue: Security weakness caused by incorrect settings → Misconfiguration

sections.title: Mobile Device Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Mobile devices become more vulnerable when users bypass security controls built into the platform. Security+ specifically includes side loading and jailbreaking.

entries.title: Side Loading
paragraphs: Side loading means installing an application from outside the normal approved application store or distribution method. The application may not have passed the platform's normal review process.
entries.memoryHook: Install the app from somewhere else.
entries.recognitionCue: Application installed outside an approved app source → Side loading

entries.title: Jailbreaking
paragraphs: Jailbreaking removes or bypasses restrictions imposed by the device manufacturer or operating system. It provides greater control but can weaken built-in security protections.
entries.memoryHook: Break out of the manufacturer's restrictions.
entries.recognitionCue: Bypass built-in mobile operating-system restrictions → Jailbreaking

sections.callout: Side loading = where the application came from · Jailbreaking = bypassing device restrictions

sections.title: Zero-Day
paragraphs: A zero-day vulnerability is newly discovered and may not yet have an effective vendor fix or sufficient defensive preparation. Attackers may exploit it before a patch is available, detection is ready, or organizations can deploy mitigations.

entries.title: Zero-Day
paragraphs: The zero-day vulnerability is the weakness. A zero-day exploit is the code or method used to attack that weakness.
A known vulnerability with an available patch is not zero-day simply because an organization failed to install the patch.
entries.memoryHook: The defenders had zero days to prepare.
entries.recognitionCue: Newly discovered vulnerability exploited before an effective fix is available → Zero-day

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: First identify where the weakness exists, then use the scenario clue to name the vulnerability.
bullets: Malicious code placed into running memory → Memory injection
Too much data written into memory → Buffer overflow
Timing or order flaw → Race condition
Object changes after validation but before use → TOC/TOU
Trusted update contains malware → Malicious update
Weakness in the operating system → OS-based
Malicious database command through input → SQLi
Malicious script runs in a victim's browser → XSS
Weakness in embedded device software → Firmware
Vendor support ended → End-of-life
Old technology still required → Legacy
Guest VM reaches host or hypervisor → VM escape
Old data remains in a reused resource → Resource reuse
Weakness tied to a cloud environment → Cloud-specific
Trusted external service compromised → Service provider
Compromised physical component → Hardware provider
Compromised software or update source → Software provider
Weak algorithm, key, or implementation → Cryptographic
Incorrect system settings → Misconfiguration
App installed outside an approved store → Side loading
Device restrictions bypassed → Jailbreaking
Newly discovered weakness without an effective fix → Zero-day

sections.title: Objective 2.3 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Buffer overflow means too much data exceeds a memory boundary. Memory injection means malicious code is deliberately placed into process memory.
A race condition is a timing or order problem. A buffer overflow is a memory-boundary problem.
SQL injection targets database interaction. Cross-site scripting executes in a browser.
Legacy means old technology remains in use. End-of-life means vendor support has ended.
VM escape breaks out of the guest environment. Resource reuse exposes leftover data in reassigned resources.
Side loading installs from an unofficial source. Jailbreaking bypasses platform restrictions.
Zero-day means newly discovered with no effective fix yet. A known vulnerability with an available but uninstalled patch is simply unpatched.
sections.callout: First identify WHERE the weakness exists. Then use the clue to identify WHAT vulnerability it is.

miniCheck.intro: Identify where each web weakness has its main effect.
miniCheck.prompt: During testing, one input changes the records returned from the application's database. In a separate test, a stored comment causes JavaScript to run in another visitor's browser.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. SQL injection turns unsafe input into a database command, while cross-site scripting causes malicious script to execute in another user's browser.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Separate the database effect from the browser effect. Review SQL Injection and Cross-Site Scripting, then try again.
